_note: Fixed five-quarter campaign: one dominant risk per quarter (rates up, stocks down, rates down, credit), then the Great Depression boss round where everything hits at once. Magnitudes are stylized approximations of the historical episodes, for Micah to verify or adjust. A shock is a vector of market moves, never a dollar loss; the engine turns it into profit and loss using each company's own balance sheet. ig_loss_pct is the credit loss rate on BBB-rated holdings (A-rated lose 15% of that rate, AAA none); hy_default_pct is the default rate on below-investment-grade bonds (40% recovery). The boss round's strength is calibrated per company and seed so that doing nothing all game collapses the company (surplus below zero); base_shock there is the shape of the crash, and the engine caps a few moves (rates no more than 4 points, stocks no more than 85%). benchmark_action is 'what a pro would do'. sample_answer is shown only in Demo mode (Jackson, seed 409), written for a quarter played with no trades.

cards.title: The Inflation Surprise
cards.signal_text: WIRE: Consumer prices ran hotter than forecast for a third straight month. Some economists say the central bank is 'behind the curve'; others expect inflation to fade on its own.
cards.headline: CENTRAL BANK HIKES AGAIN; BOND YIELDS SURGE
cards.narrative: Rates jumped across the curve in a matter of weeks. Dealers, repo lenders and securities-lending counterparties all demanded more collateral, and competitors now pay more on new annuities, so policyholders are surrendering too. Cash is flying out the door, and bonds sold to raise it fetch less than they cost. Stocks barely moved.
cards.lesson: When rates rise fast, bonds and liabilities both fall in value, and for a life insurer the mismatch can even help. The real danger is cash. Counterparties demand more collateral the same week, policyholders surrender to chase higher rates, and swaps that gain when rates fall now lose money. Collateral you post is still yours but it is locked up, so your liquidity ratio drops, and without cash on hand you sell bonds at fire-sale prices to meet the calls.
cards.source_note: Stylized on 2022, when the US 10-year Treasury yield rose roughly 2.3 percentage points over the year and the UK's September gilt crisis showed how fast collateral calls can drain cash. A typical draw (1.0x) here is a 0.6 percentage point rise in rates, collateral calls of 2% of invested assets and surrenders at twice the normal pace.
cards.sample_answer: Interest rates jumped, and that was the main driver. Our liabilities are longer than our assets, so their value fell more than our bonds did, which actually lifted surplus. Stocks dipped a little as the second factor, raising our guarantee costs. The real danger was cash: dealers demanded collateral and policyholders surrendered, which pushed our liquidity ratio below the floor. More cash on hand would have covered the calls without fire sales.

real_world.title: 2022: the fastest rate hikes in 40 years
real_world.text: Inflation hit its highest level in four decades and the Federal Reserve raised rates at the fastest pace since the early 1980s. The 10-year Treasury yield rose by more than 2 percentage points over the year. In September, UK pension funds using interest rate swaps faced collateral calls so large they had to dump government bonds, and the Bank of England stepped in. Annuity holders cashed out to chase higher rates elsewhere.

cards.title: The Bubble Bursts
cards.signal_text: WIRE: Tech stocks trade at record multiples of earnings. A few strategists warn the rally is running on hype; most say this time is different.
cards.headline: STOCKS PLUNGE AS THE TECH BUBBLE BURSTS
cards.narrative: Stocks plunged in a few weeks as investors gave up on sky-high valuations. Customers' variable annuity accounts shrank, so the guarantees we wrote on them are now worth much more, and our own stock and private equity holdings fell too. Bonds barely moved.
cards.lesson: A variable annuity guarantee is a promise to pay when markets fall: when stocks drop, what you owe rises at exactly the wrong time, on top of losses on your own stock holdings. Stock-market puts pay off in that same fall. They cost a premium every quarter, which is why you buy them before the crash, not after.
cards.source_note: Stylized on 2000-2002, when the S&P 500 fell about 49% from peak to trough. One quarter here compresses part of that: a typical draw (1.0x) is a stock fall of a little over 20%.
cards.sample_answer: Stocks crashed, and that was the main driver. Falling markets shrank customers' annuity accounts, so the guarantees we wrote became more expensive for us, and our own stock and alternative holdings fell too. Rates dipped slightly as the second factor, which hurt a little because our liabilities are longer than our assets. Stock-market puts would have offset most of the guarantee loss.

real_world.title: 2000-2002: the dot-com bust
real_world.text: After a boom in internet stocks, the Nasdaq fell nearly 80% from its March 2000 peak and the S&P 500 lost about half its value by late 2002. Insurers that had sold variable annuities with generous guarantees saw what they owed jump just as their own stock holdings fell.

cards.title: Lower for Longer
cards.signal_text: WIRE: Growth is slowing and inflation keeps undershooting the target. Bond traders are betting the central bank will cut rates, possibly a lot.
cards.headline: RATES TUMBLE TO RECORD LOWS
cards.narrative: The central bank cut rates and long bond yields fell to record lows. Our promises to policyholders stretch decades into the future, further than our bonds, so their value rose by more than our bonds did. Guarantees got more expensive too. Policyholders are happy to stay put.
cards.lesson: When rates fall, long liabilities rise in value by more than shorter bonds: that duration gap is a life insurer's main rate risk. Interest rate swaps that gain when rates fall close the gap. The catch is the one you met when rates rose: the same swaps lose money, and demand collateral, when rates go up.
cards.source_note: Stylized on 2019-2020, when the US 10-year Treasury yield fell about 2.7 percentage points. A typical draw (1.0x) here is a 1 percentage point fall in one quarter.
cards.sample_answer: Interest rates fell sharply, and that was the main driver. Our liabilities are longer than our assets, so their value rose more than our bonds did and surplus fell. Stocks dipped a little as the second factor. Rate swaps that gain when rates fall would have closed most of that gap.

real_world.title: 2019-2020: rates fall toward zero
real_world.text: Slowing growth in 2019 and then the pandemic pushed US interest rates to record lows: the 10-year Treasury yield fell from about 3.2% in late 2018 to near 0.5% in 2020. Long promises made at higher rates became far more expensive to back, and several large life insurers took big charges on their guaranteed products.

cards.title: The Junk Bond Rout
cards.signal_text: WIRE: Oil prices have halved in a year. Energy companies borrowed heavily when oil was expensive, and rating agencies are starting to downgrade them.
cards.headline: JUNK BONDS CRASH AS DEFAULTS MOUNT
cards.narrative: A wave of defaults hit oil and gas companies and investors dumped risky corporate bonds. Our below-investment-grade bonds lost value and some issuers stopped paying altogether. Weaker investment-grade bonds and commercial mortgages took smaller losses. Stocks dipped, and government bond yields fell as money fled to safety.
cards.lesson: Credit risk has two parts: spreads widen, marking bonds down, and some borrowers default, which is a permanent loss. An insurer holding bonds to maturity can ride out much of the spread move, but not the defaults. Moving the riskiest bonds into government bonds before the storm gives up some yield: that is the price of sleeping at night.
cards.source_note: Stylized on 2015-2016, when US high-yield spreads rose from about 3.5 to over 8 percentage points. A typical draw (1.0x) here widens high-yield spreads by 3 percentage points with 3% of junk bonds defaulting.
cards.sample_answer: Defaults were the main driver: junk-bond issuers stopped paying, which is a permanent credit loss, unlike spreads widening. Stocks dipped as the second factor, which raised our guarantee costs a bit. Moving risky bonds into government bonds before the rout would have cut the default losses.

real_world.title: 2015-2016: the energy credit rout
real_world.text: Oil fell from over $100 a barrel in mid-2014 to under $30 in early 2016. Dozens of heavily indebted energy companies defaulted, high-yield bond spreads more than doubled, and investors pulled money out of junk bond funds.

cards.title: The Great Depression
cards.signal_text: WIRE: Stocks have doubled in two years, much of it on borrowed money. Banks are lending freely. Quietly, farm prices and factory orders have started to fall.
cards.headline: CRASH! BANKS FAIL, DEFAULTS SOAR, A DEALER GOES UNDER
cards.narrative: Everything broke at once. Stocks collapsed, companies stopped paying their debts, property loans went bad and investors piled into government bonds, driving yields down. One of our derivatives dealers failed, and frightened policyholders want their money back.
cards.lesson: In a true crisis the risks you managed one at a time all hit together, and they feed each other: falling stocks raise guarantee costs, defaults eat capital, falling rates raise liabilities, and the scramble for cash forces sales at fire-sale prices. No single hedge saves you. Survival comes from having every defense in place before the storm, including collateral and more than one dealer.
cards.source_note: Stylized on 1929-1933 and late 2008, compressed into one quarter. The boss round's strength is set for each company so that doing nothing all game wipes out its equity; a well-hedged company survives.
cards.sample_answer: Everything crashed at once. Stocks collapsed, and that was the main driver: our stock and alternative holdings fell and the market guarantees we wrote became far more expensive. Rates also plunged, the second factor, which hurt because our liabilities are longer than our assets. Defaults and a failed dealer piled on. We had no protection, so our equity was wiped out; puts, swaps and moving risky bonds to government bonds would all have helped.

real_world.title: 1929-1933: the Great Depression
real_world.text: The stock market crashed in October 1929 and kept falling: by mid-1932 stocks had lost almost 90% from their peak. Thousands of banks failed, corporate defaults soared and US output fell by about a quarter. Investors fled to the safety of government bonds.
